To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is no evidence that the incidence or prevalence of mental disorders is greater in the UK among migrants from the New Commonwealth or the Caribbean than it is among the indigenous population, or among migrants from Europe, North America, Australasia or Asia.
the rates of schizophrenia in the West Indian population of the UK are high, and that the rates of the disorder in the second generation of immigrants are higher than in the first generation.
The rate of schizophrenia among second generation immigrants from the Caribbean is approximately double that of first generation immigrants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between migration, social class and mental illness.
the aetiology of schizophrenia, with a focus on the relationship between the disorder and migration.
the aetiological role of perinatal infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
schizophrenia is not an immigrant disease.
schizophrenia is a genetically determined disease, but that its expression is modified by environmental factors.

the relationship between schizophrenia and migration has not yet been fully explained, but that the evidence for an association is strong, that the most plausible explanation of the phenomenon is that it is aetiological rather than epidemiological, and that the most plausible aetiology is obstetric complications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the increased rates of schizophrenia found among immigrants are due to environmental causes, notably the effects of obstetric complications and infections, which are more common among the children of immigrants than among their host country compatriots, and which increase the risk of schizophrenia in the offspring.

the higher prevalence of schizophrenia among second generation West Indians is not a result of the migration experience but rather a result of the genetic background of the parents who migrated from the Caribbean to the UK.

the risk of schizophrenia is higher among immigrants than non-immigrants, that the difference is greater among second-generation immigrants than among first-generation immigrants, that the risk is higher among immigrants from developing than from developed countries, and that the difference is larger for men than for women.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to look beyond psychosocial explanations when trying to account for the increased risk of psychosis among immigrants.

the risk of psychosis is increased in the second generation of migrants, but not in the first generation, and that this increase is not associated with the degree of acculturation of the first-generation migrants.
there are a number of factors, including genetic and environmental, which may influence the risk of developing schizophrenia in a second-generation immigrant.
